extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining patentability where claims involve printed matter, machine‑readable media, inherency, and product/process distinctions; explains when printed matter or inherent properties are given patentable weight and who bears evidence burdens. Intended to guide examiners in applying 35 U.S.C. 101/102/103 standards and related case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider all claim limitations; cannot disregard printed matter
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO personnel must consider all claim limitations when determining patentability of an invention over the prior art. Since a claim must be read as a whole, USPTO personnel may not disregard claim limitations that include printed matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Gulack and Diamond v. Diehr. The examiner must treat printed matter as a claim limitation in the overall claim construction analysis; do not ignore printed matter when comparing to prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed matter — threshold: limitation directed to content of information
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation is printed matter only if it claims the content of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the first step of printed matter analysis (In re DiStefano). If the limitation is directed to content, proceed to determine whether it is functionally or structurally related to its substrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional relationship test for printed matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Printed matter and associated product must be in a functional relationship to be given patentable weight; a functional relationship can be found where the printed matter performs some function with respect to the product or the product performs some function with respect to the printed matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: indicia on a measuring cup indicating volume (In re Miller); a hatband whose physical arrangement of numbers satisfies a claimed algorithm (Gulack). If such a new and nonobvious functional relationship exists, give patentable weight to the printed matter (In re Lowry, In re Ngai, In re Gulack).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence against functional relationship (support-only printed matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: No functional relationship exists where a product merely serves as a support for printed matter or where the claim as a whole is directed to conveying a message/meaning to a human independent of the substrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: hatband images not arranged in sequence (Gulack); deck of playing cards with images (In re Bryan); measuring tape with unrelated wiring information; kit containing chemicals plus general printed instructions that are unrelated to that specific set (In re Ngai). If printed matter and product do not depend on each other, printed matter lacks functional relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional relationship must be new and nonobvious to carry patentable weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a functional relationship between printed matter and product is found, the relationship must be new and nonobvious for the printed matter to be given patentable weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a functional relationship exists (e.g., color-coded indicia indicating expiration date), the claim may be anticipated or obvious if prior art teaches the claimed invention or combination of references shows it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-readable media: evaluate programming-system relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining the scope of a claim directed to a computer-readable medium containing programming, examine the relationship between the programming and the intended computer system to determine functional relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the programming performs some function with respect to the intended computer system (e.g., attribute data objects facilitating retrieval), a functional relationship exists and the claimed artifact is given patentable weight (Lowry). If the medium merely supports information directed to a human reader (e.g., batting averages, music tracks), no functional relationship exists. Claims reciting executable code that embody an abstract idea must also be evaluated for eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 (see MPEP § 2106).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency may be relied upon in 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: The express, implicit, and inherent disclosures of a prior art reference may be relied upon in rejecting claims under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103; inherency is a question of fact and can arise in anticipation and obviousness contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Napier and In re Grasselli. Examiner may assert that prior art inherently discloses a claimed feature even if not expressly stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of a new property of old subject matter does not render it patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of a previously unappreciated property of a prior art composition, or a scientific explanation for the prior art's functioning, does not make the old composition patentably new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Atlas Powder Co. and In re Best. Finding a new use, property, or function that was inherently present in prior art does not by itself confer patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent feature need not have been recognized at relevant time
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no requirement that a person of ordinary skill in the art would have recognized the inherently present feature at the relevant time; it only matters that the subject matter is in fact inherent in the prior art reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Schering, Toro, Abbott Labs, SmithKline Beecham, In re Omeprazole. Post‑critical date evidence may show inherency; inherent structures/functions can exist even if unrecognized previously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation/obviousness OK when prior art appears identical though silent on inherent characteristic
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 can be made when the prior art product seems identical to the claimed composition except the prior art is silent as to an inherent characteristic, because a prior art product that inherently possesses each claimed limitation anticipates the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Best and related reasoning: a single reference can anticipate even if it does not state the characteristic explicitly, if the characteristic is necessarily present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must provide rationale/evidence to support inherency
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that a result or characteristic may occur in the prior art is not sufficient; the examiner must provide a basis in fact and/or technical reasoning to reasonably support that the characteristic necessarily flows from the teachings of the applied prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Ex parte Levy and PAR Pharmaceutical v. TWI. Inherency in an obviousness analysis requires that the limitation necessarily be present or be the natural result of combining prior art elements. An 'invitation to investigate' is not inherency (Metabolite Labs.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Once examiner shows inherency, burden of production shifts to applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reference teaching a product appearing substantially identical is made the basis of a rejection and the examiner presents evidence or reasoning to show inherency, the burden of production shifts to the applicant to prove the prior art products do not necessarily or inherently possess the characteristics of the claimed product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Best and In re Fitzgerald. Applicant must present objective evidence to rebut (e.g., comparative data, specific dimensions/tests). Declarations lacking essential factual specifics (e.g., Schreiber) may fail to rebut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product/apparatus claims: substantially identical structure/composition implies properties/functions presumed inherent
rubrics_metrics.description: Where claimed and prior art products are identical or substantially identical in structure or composition, or are produced by identical or substantially identical processes, a prima facie case of anticipation or obviousness is established and claimed properties/functions are presumed inherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Best, In re Spada, Titanium Metals Corp. Applicant bears burden to show the prior art product does not possess the characteristics; examples include chemical composition matches or structural identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition claims: identical composition implies same properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Products of identical chemical composition cannot have mutually exclusive properties; if the prior art teaches the same composition, applicant's disclosed/claimed properties are necessarily present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Spada. Composition and its properties are inseparable; assertions of differing properties require objective evidence to rebut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product claims: nonfunctional printed matter does not distinguish over otherwise identical prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the only difference between a prior art product and a claimed product is printed matter that is not functionally related to the product, the content of the printed matter will not distinguish the claimed product from the prior art for patentability purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Ngai, In re Gulack, In re Miller, In re Xiao, In re Bryan. Court rationale: permitting such distinctions would allow perpetual patenting by adding new instruction sheets or labels unless a new and nonobvious functional relationship exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims: prior art device may anticipate method if device inherently performs method in normal operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under inherency principles, if a prior art device, in its normal and usual operation, would necessarily perform the method claimed, then the method is anticipated by the prior art device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re King and In re Best. When prior art device is the same as the device described in the specification for carrying out the claimed method, it can be assumed the device will inherently perform the claimed process. Applicant must introduce evidence (e.g., demonstrating differences) to rebut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process-of-use claims: new and nonobvious uses of old structures may be patentable, but mere discovery of new property may not
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of a new use for an old structure based on unknown properties might be patentable as a process of use; however, when the claim recites using an old composition/structure and the 'use' is directed to a result or property of that composition/structure, the claim is anticipated if the prior art composition/structure is the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Hack and In re May. Applicants relying on unexpected properties must show they are nonobvious and unexpected; a mere finding of a previously unknown property does not necessarily make a new use patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims: scope defined by structure implied by steps, not by the manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Product-by-process claims are not limited to the manipulations of the recited steps but are limited to the structure implied by those steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: when evaluating novelty/obviousness of product-by-process claims, focus on the structural identity resulting from the process; see MPEP § 2113 for further guidance on burden and analogous issues.
